claim: To attach a separately-built handle (or any curved-end detail) precisely onto a curved body: build the handle roughly in place, select just the small cluster of end-cap faces that need to touch the body, assign them to a Vertex Group, add a Shrinkwrap modifier on the handle targeting the body mesh, set the Shrinkwrap's Vertex Group to that group (so only the end-cap faces are pulled onto the surface, not the whole handle), and set the wrap method to 'Project' constrained to a single relevant axis -- this snaps just the contact points flush to the body's actual curvature instead of eyeballing the fit or flattening the whole handle onto the surface.
supporting_evidence: Direct quotes (9:38-10:34): "Now we can shrink wrap our handle to the cup... Now it's done exactly what it says on the tin, and it's just flattened everything against the mug. However, we only really want to snap the ends of the handle here. So jumping into edit mode, we can select these four polygons here, go over to our vertex options and just add a group... Now jumping out into object mode, going back over to our modifiers, we can select that group, vertex group... here now we have only those vertices snapping, but it's not doing so in a massively elegant way, so let's just change the nearest surface method to project, and we want it on one axis only"
rejected_alternative: Shrinkwrapping the whole handle object with no vertex group (flattens the entire handle onto the body surface instead of just the contact points)
reason: An unrestricted shrinkwrap collapses the whole handle's shape onto the body surface; restricting it to a vertex group covering only the actual contact faces preserves the handle's intended form while still snapping the attachment points exactly flush.

claim: Object transforms (rotation and scale) must be applied (Ctrl+A) before Boolean, Bevel, Solidify, or Shrinkwrap modifiers are added -- otherwise these modifiers behave inconsistently across axes or fail outright (a Shrinkwrap's axis-restricted projection direction is defined in the object's local space, so un-applied rotation/scale points it the wrong way).
supporting_evidence: Stated and demonstrated twice: (6:55) "we need to apply the scale here as it's all gone a bit awry, so to do so we can ctrl and a, apply rotation and scale, so that modifiers like bevel work proportionately on all axes"; and later, a shrinkwrap silently fails until transforms are applied: "it's not working. This is because we forgot to apply our rotation and scale... Now it's working."

claim: To get a genuinely hard/crisp edge under a Subdivision Surface modifier without modeling extra bevel geometry by hand: select the edge loop that should stay sharp and apply Edge Crease (Shift+E), then still add Shade Auto Smooth and a separate Bevel *modifier* afterward in the stack for the final render-quality edge -- crease alone controls how tightly SubD pulls to that edge, while the bevel modifier adds the physical small chamfer on top.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (12:44 area): "Now we want a hard edge along the side here, so we can alt and click to select these edge loops on both sides, and then with shift and e we create a crease, like so... let's give it the shade smooth treatment with right click, shade auto smooth, and also add a bevel modifier after our sub d modifier"

claim: 'Bool Tool' add-on's non-destructive 'Brush > Slice' boolean mode (Ctrl+Shift+B after selecting cutter then target) splits a mesh into two separate pieces along the cutter boundary without deleting either side and without leaving a permanent boolean modifier -- useful for carving a sci-fi panel-line style cut into a hard-surface part while keeping both resulting halves as real, separately-bevelable geometry.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~20:20-20:41): "we could take advantage of another add-on that ships with Blender called bool tool... this just enables us to select our cutter here, select the thing we want to cut and then control and shift and B, and then we activate our bool tool. And this time we want to use the brush boolean, which is the non-destructive way of doing this and select slice. Now we have two elements to our leg here"

claim: For a bilaterally symmetric assembly built from several separate objects (e.g. a robot's two legs), duplicate the whole set with Alt+D (linked duplicate, sharing mesh data so a later edit to one side updates both), snap the 3D cursor to the world origin, set the transform pivot to the 3D cursor, then Ctrl+M and the axis key to mirror-flip the duplicate across that origin -- faster and more consistent than manually rebuilding or individually mirroring each part.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~23:36): "All we need to do is snap our cursor into world origin with shift and S, select all of our leg elements like so. Make sure that our transform pivot space is on 3D cursor and then ALT and D to duplicate all of our elements, right click to drop and then CTRL and M and then X to flip that about our X axis"
rejected_alternative: Manually mirroring or rebuilding each leg part individually
